nodes.name: Naive height of an integer polynomial
nodes.statement: The (na\"\i ve) height $H(P)$ of an integer polynomial $P(x)$ is the maximum of the absolute values of its coefficients.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.genus: the maximum of the absolute values of its coefficients

nodes.name: Root separation sep(P) and exponent e(P)
nodes.statement: For a separable integer polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $d \ge 2$ and with distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_d$, we set $$ {\rm sep}(P) = \min_{1 \le i < j \le d} \, |\alpha_i - \alpha_j| $$ and define the quantity $e(P)$ by $$ {\rm sep}(P) = H(P)^{-e(P)}. $$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: sep(P) is the minimal distance between distinct roots of P; e(P) is defined by sep(P)=H(P)^{-e(P)}.

nodes.name: Root separation exponents e(d) and e_irr(d)
nodes.statement: Following the notation introduced in \cite{BM2}, for $d \ge 2$, we set $$ e(d) := \limsup_{{\rm deg}(P) = d, H(P) \to + \infty} e(P) $$ and $$ e_{{\rm irr}} (d) := \limsup_{{\rm deg}(P) = d, H(P) \to + \infty} e(P), $$ where the latter limsup is taken over the irreducible integer polynomials $P(x)$ of degree $d$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: e(d) (resp. e_irr(d)) is the limsup of e(P) over integer (resp. irreducible integer) polynomials of degree d as H(P) grows.

nodes.name: Monic root separation exponents e*(d) and e*_irr(d)
nodes.statement: We further define $e^*(d)$ and $e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d)$ by restricting to monic, respectively, monic irreducible integer polynomials, of degree $d$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Trivial comparison of root separation exponents
nodes.statement: Obviously, we have $$ e(d) \ge e_{{\rm irr}}(d) \quad \mbox{and} \quad e^*(d) \ge e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d), \quad (d \ge 2). $$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: e(d) \ge e_{{\rm irr}}(d) \quad \mbox{and} \quad e^*(d) \ge e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d),

nodes.name: Mahler's root separation bound
nodes.statement: A classical result of Mahler \cite{Mah64} asserts that $e(d) \le d-1$ for every $d \ge 2$ and it is easy to check that $e_{{\rm irr}}(2)=e(2)=1$ and $e^*(2)=e_{{\rm irr}}^*(2) = 0$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Mahler: e(d) <= d-1 for all d >= 2; also e(2)=e_irr(2)=1 and e*(2)=e*_irr(2)=0.

nodes.name: Evertse-Schonhage theorem e(3)=2
nodes.statement: Evertse \cite{Ev} and Sch\"onhage \cite{Sch} proved, independently, that $e_{{\rm irr}}(3)=e(3)=2$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Previously known lower bounds for root separation exponents
nodes.statement: The following inequalities gather the lower bounds obtained by Beresnevich, Bernik, Bugeaud, Dujella, G\"otze, and Mignotte in the four papers \cite{BM1,BM2,BBG,BD}: $$ e_{{\rm irr}}(d) \geq \frac{d}{2} +\frac{d-2}{4(d-1)}, \quad \mbox{for $d\geq 4$}, $$ $$ e (d) \geq \frac{d+1}{2}, \quad \mbox{for odd $d\geq 5$}, $$ $$ e^*(3)=e_{{\rm irr}}^*(3) \geq \frac{3}{2}, \quad e^* (5) \ge 2, \quad e_{{\rm irr}}^*(5) \ge \frac{7}{4}, $$ $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{d}{2}, \quad e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d) \geq \frac{d-1}{2}, \quad \mbox{for even $d\geq 4$}, $$ and $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{d-1}{2}, \quad e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d)\geq \frac{d}{2} +\frac{d-2}{4(d-1)} - 1, \quad \mbox{for odd $d\geq 7$}. $$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.origin_citation: Bugeaud & Mignotte 2004, 2010; Beresnevich, Bernik & Gotze 2010; Bugeaud & Dujella 2011
nodes.statement_short: Earlier lower bounds of order d/2 for e(d), e_irr(d), e*(d), e*_irr(d) in various parity ranges.

nodes.name: Theorem 1: lower bound for e(d)
nodes.statement: For any integer $d\geq 4$, we have $$ e(d) \geq \frac{2d-1}{3}. $$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.label: tm1

nodes.name: Theorem 2: lower bound for e*(d)
nodes.statement: For any even positive integer $d\geq 6$, we have $$ e^*(d) \geq \frac{2d-3}{3}. $$ For any odd positive integer $d\geq 7$, we have $$ e^*(d) \geq \frac{2d-5}{3}. $$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.label: tm2

nodes.name: Linear polynomial L_n
nodes.statement: For an integer $d \ge 4$, the reducible polynomials arising in the proof of Theorem 1 are products of a linear polynomial $L_n (x) = (n^2 + 3n +1)x - (n+2)$ with an irreducible polynomial $p_{d-1, n} (x)$ of degree $d-1$ and height of order $n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The reducible polynomials for Theorem 1 are L_n(x)=(n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2) times an irreducible p_{d-1,n}(x) of degree d-1 and height ~n.

nodes.name: Application to Bombieri's Thue-Siegel principle
nodes.statement: Say differently, we construct a parametric family $(y_{d,n})_{n \ge 1}$ of algebraic numbers of degree $d-1$ which are very well approximated by a rational number with large height (in comparison to the height of $y_{d,n}$). This means that it is then possible to apply Bombieri's version of the Thue--Siegel principle \cite[Theorem 4]{Bom} to the anchor pair $(y_{d,n}, x_n)$ to derive a rather good effective irrationality measure for $y_{d,n}$ when $n$ is sufficiently large in comparison to $d$. In his paper, Bombieri used the polynomials $x^d - n x + 1$, which have a root very close to the rational number $1/n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The algebraic numbers y_{d,n} are very well approximated by rationals, so Bombieri's Thue-Siegel principle gives effective irrationality measures.

nodes.name: Theorem 3: lower bound for e*_irr(d)
nodes.statement: For any positive integer $d\geq 4$, we have $$ e_{{\rm irr}}^* (d) \geq \frac{d}{2}-\frac{1}{4}. $$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.label: tm3

nodes.name: Convention on implied constants
nodes.statement: Throughout the next sections, the constants implied by the symbols $O$, $\ll$ and $\gg$ can be explicitly computed, are independent of the parameter $n$, and depend at most on the degree $d$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: We want to construct a one-parametric sequence of integer polynomials $p_{d,n}(x)$ of degree $d$ having a root very close to the rational number $x_n=(n+2)/(n^2+3n+1)$. Then the polynomials $$ P_{d,n}(x)=((n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)) p_{d-1,n}(x) $$ will have two roots very close to each other. We define the sequence $p_{d,n}(x)$ recursively by $$ \eqalign{ & p_{0,n} (x) = -1, \quad p_{1,n} (x) = (n+1)x-1, \cr & p_{d,n} (x) = (1+x) p_{d-1,n}(x) +x^2 p_{d-2,n} (x). \cr} \eqno (1) $$ We claim that $$ p_{d,n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n^2+3n+1}\right) = \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{(n^2+3n+1)^d}. \eqno (2) $$ Indeed, (2) is clearly true for $d=0$ and $d=1$. Assume now that $d \ge 1$ is an integer for which (2) holds for $p_{d-1,n} (x)$ and $p_{d,n} (x)$. Then we deduce from the recursion (1) that $$ \eqalign{ p_{d,n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n^2+3n+1}\right) & = \frac{(-1)^{d-2}}{(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \cdot \frac{n^2+ 4n+3}{n^2+3n+1} \cr & \, \, \, \, \, \, \, \, + \frac{(-1)^{d-3}}{(n^2+3n+1)^{d-2}} \cdot \frac{n^2+ 4n+4}{(n^2+3n+1)^2} \cr & = \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{(n^2+3n+1)^d}, \cr} $$ as claimed. We now show that for sufficiently large $n$ the polynomial $p_{d,n} (x)$ has a root between $x_n$ and $$ z_{d,n}=x_n + \frac{(-1)^{d}}{n(n^2+3n+1)^d}. $$ Observe that $$ (-1)^{d-1} p_{d,n}(x_n) = \frac{1}{(n^2+3n+1)^d} > 0. $$ By Rolle's theorem, there exists $z'_{d,n}$ between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}$ such that $$ p_{d,n}(z_{d,n})=p_{d,n}(x_n)+(z_{d,n}-x_n)p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}). $$ It follows easily by induction that $$ p_{d,n}(x)=-1+(n-d+2)x+((d-1)n-(d-1)(d-2)/2)x^2+\cdots $$ Since $x_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) = n + d + O(1/n)$. Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) > n$. This implies that $$ (-1)^{d-1}p_{d,n}(z_{d,n}) = \frac{1}{(n^2+3n+1)^d} - \frac{1}{n(n^2+3n+1)^d}p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) < 0. $$ Therefore, the polynomial $P_{d,n}(x)=((n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)) p_{d-1,n}(x)$ has two close roots: $x_n$ and $y_{d,n}$, which is between $x_n$ and $z_{d-1,n}$. This yields $$ {\rm sep}(P_{d,n}) \leq |x_n - y_{d,n} | \leq \frac{1}{n(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \leq \frac{1}{n^{2d-1}}, \eqno (3) $$ when $n$ is large enough. Since the height of $P_{d,n} (x)$ is bounded from above by $n^3$ times a number depending only on $d$, this gives $$ e(d)\geq \frac{2d-1}{3}, $$ by letting $n$ tend to infinity. The proof of Theorem \ref{tm1} is complete.

nodes.statement: We claim that $$ p_{d,n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n^2+3n+1}\right) = \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{(n^2+3n+1)^d}. \eqno (2) $$ Indeed, (2) is clearly true for $d=0$ and $d=1$. nodes.name: Separation bound (3)
nodes.statement: Therefore, the polynomial $P_{d,n}(x)=((n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)) p_{d-1,n}(x)$ has two close roots: $x_n$ and $y_{d,n}$, which is between $x_n$ and $z_{d-1,n}$. nodes.statement_short: Height ~n^3 with (3) gives e(d) >= (2d-1)/3.

nodes.name: Irreducibility of p_{d-1,n}
nodes.statement: By Gelfond's inequality (see e.g. \cite[Lemma A.3]{BuLiv}), the height of $y_{d,n}$ is $\ll n$. Liouville's inequality (see e.g. \cite[Theorem A.1]{BuLiv}) then implies that $$ |x_n - y_{d,n}| \gg n^{-2 \delta-1}, $$ where $\delta$ denotes the degree of $y_{d,n}$. Combined with (3), this gives $\delta = d-1$ and establishes that the polynomial $p_{d-1,n} (x)$ must be irreducible.

nodes.statement_short: Gelfond's and Liouville's inequalities combined with (3) force deg y_{d,n}=d-1, so p_{d-1,n} is irreducible.

nodes.name: Sharpness of Liouville's inequality
nodes.statement: Also, (3) shows that Liouville's inequality $$ |x_n - y_{d,n}| \gg n^{-2d+1} $$ is sharp in terms of $n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: In order to get a family of monic polynomials with similar separation properties as the family $P_{d,n}(x)$, we replace the linear non-monic polynomial $L_n(x)=(n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)$ by the monic quadratic polynomial $$ K_n(x)=x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2). $$ Thus, we want to construct a one-parametric sequence of integer polynomials $q_{d,n}(x)$ of degree $d$ having a root very close to the root $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$ of $K_n(x)$. Then the polynomials $$ Q_{d,n}(x)=(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-2,n}(x) $$ will have two roots very close to each other. For $d \ge 0$ even, we define the sequence $q_{d,n}(x)$ recursively by $$ \eqalign{ & q_{0,n} (x) = 1, \quad q_{2,n} (x) = x^2-(n+1)x+1, \cr & q_{d,n} (x) = (2x^2 + x + 1) q_{d-2,n} (x) - x^4 q_{d-4,n} (x). \cr} \eqno (4) $$ We claim that $q_{d,n} (x)- q_{d-2,n} (x) q_{2,n} (x)$ is divisible by $K_n (x)$. This is easy to check for $d=2$ and $d=4$, and then the claim follows by induction using the recursion (4). This yields that $$ q_{d,n}(y_n) = q_{d-2,n}(y_n)q_{2,n}(y_n) = (q_{2,n}(y_n))^{d/2}, $$ for $d \ge 2$ even. From $$ y_n=1/n-1/n^2+2/n^3-4/n^4+8/n^5+ O(1/n^6), $$ we get $q_{2,n}(y_n)=1/n^4 + O(1/n^5)$ and hence $$ q_{d,n}(y_n) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}). $$ We now show that for sufficiently large $n$ the polynomial $q_{d,n} (x)$ has a root between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}=y_n + \frac{2}{n^{2d+1}}$. We have $$ q_{d,n}(y_n) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}) > 0. $$ By Rolle's theorem, there exists $w'_{d,n}$ between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$ such that $$ q_{d,n}(w_{d,n})=q_{d,n}(y_n)+(w_{d,n}-y_n)q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}). $$ It follows easily by induction that $$ q_{d,n}(x)=1+(-n+d/2-2)x+((-d/2+1)n+(d^2-2d+8)/8)x^2+\cdots $$ Since $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) = -n - d/2 + O(1/n)$. Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < -n$. This implies $$ q_{d,n}(w_{d,n}) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}) + \frac{2}{n^{2d+1}}q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < 0. $$ Thus, the polynomial $Q_{d,n}(x)=(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-2,n}(x)$ has two close roots: $y_n$ and $v_{d,n}$, which is between $y_n$ and $w_{d-2,n}$. This yields $$ {\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-3}}, $$ when $n$ is large enough. Since $H(Q_{d,n})=O(n^3)$, this gives $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-3}{3}, $$ by letting $n$ tend to infinity. Let now $d$ be odd. Then we define $$ Q_{d,n}(x)=x(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-3,n}(x). $$ This polynomial has two close roots: $y_n$ and a root lying between $y_n$ and $w_{d-3,n}$. Thus we get $$ {\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-5}}, $$ for $n$ large enough, and $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-5}{3}. $$ The proof of Theorem \ref{tm2} is complete.

nodes.name: Monic construction goal
nodes.statement: In order to get a family of monic polynomials with similar separation properties as the family $P_{d,n}(x)$, we replace the linear non-monic polynomial $L_n(x)=(n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)$ by the monic quadratic polynomial $$ K_n(x)=x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2). $$ Thus, we want to construct a one-parametric sequence of integer polynomials $q_{d,n}(x)$ of degree $d$ having a root very close to the root $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$ of $K_n(x)$. Then the polynomials $$ Q_{d,n}(x)=(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-2,n}(x) $$ will have two roots very close to each other.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Introduce K_n and the target family Q_{d,n}.

nodes.name: Recursive definition of q_{d,n}
nodes.statement: For $d \ge 0$ even, we define the sequence $q_{d,n}(x)$ recursively by $$ \eqalign{ & q_{0,n} (x) = 1, \quad q_{2,n} (x) = x^2-(n+1)x+1, \cr & q_{d,n} (x) = (2x^2 + x + 1) q_{d-2,n} (x) - x^4 q_{d-4,n} (x). \cr} \eqno (4) $$
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Define q_{d,n} by recursion (4).

nodes.name: Divisibility claim
nodes.statement: We claim that $q_{d,n} (x)- q_{d-2,n} (x) q_{2,n} (x)$ is divisible by $K_n (x)$. This is easy to check for $d=2$ and $d=4$, and then the claim follows by induction using the recursion (4).
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: K_n divides q_{d,n}-q_{d-2,n}q_{2,n}, by induction.

nodes.name: Value at y_n
nodes.statement: This yields that $$ q_{d,n}(y_n) = q_{d-2,n}(y_n)q_{2,n}(y_n) = (q_{2,n}(y_n))^{d/2}, $$ for $d \ge 2$ even.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Hence q_{d,n}(y_n)=q_{2,n}(y_n)^{d/2}.

nodes.name: Asymptotics of q_{d,n}(y_n)
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotics give q_{d,n}(y_n) ~ n^{-2d}.

nodes.name: Root between y_n and w_{d,n}
nodes.statement: We now show that for sufficiently large $n$ the polynomial $q_{d,n} (x)$ has a root between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}=y_n + \frac{2}{n^{2d+1}}$. We have $$ q_{d,n}(y_n) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}) > 0. $$ By Rolle's theorem, there exists $w'_{d,n}$ between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$ such that $$ q_{d,n}(w_{d,n})=q_{d,n}(y_n)+(w_{d,n}-y_n)q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}). $$ It follows easily by induction that $$ q_{d,n}(x)=1+(-n+d/2-2)x+((-d/2+1)n+(d^2-2d+8)/8)x^2+\cdots $$ Since $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) = -n - d/2 + O(1/n)$. Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < -n$. This implies $$ q_{d,n}(w_{d,n}) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}) + \frac{2}{n^{2d+1}}q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < 0. $$
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Show q_{d,n} has a root between y_n and w_{d,n} by a sign change.

nodes.name: Sign at y_n
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Positive at y_n.

nodes.name: Mean value theorem
nodes.statement: By Rolle's theorem, there exists $w'_{d,n}$ between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$ such that $$ q_{d,n}(w_{d,n})=q_{d,n}(y_n)+(w_{d,n}-y_n)q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}). $$
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Mean value expansion.

nodes.name: Expansion of q_{d,n}
nodes.statement: It follows easily by induction that $$ q_{d,n}(x)=1+(-n+d/2-2)x+((-d/2+1)n+(d^2-2d+8)/8)x^2+\cdots $$
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Low-order coefficients of q_{d,n}.

nodes.name: Derivative bound
nodes.statement: Since $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) = -n - d/2 + O(1/n)$. Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < -n$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Derivative below -n.

nodes.name: Sign at w_{d,n}
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Negative at w_{d,n}: sign change.

nodes.name: Separation bound, even d
nodes.statement: Thus, the polynomial $Q_{d,n}(x)=(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-2,n}(x)$ has two close roots: $y_n$ and $v_{d,n}$, which is between $y_n$ and $w_{d-2,n}$. This yields $$ {\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-3}}, $$ when $n$ is large enough.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Q_{d,n} has two close roots with sep <= 2n^{-(2d-3)}.

nodes.name: Conclude even case
nodes.statement: Since $H(Q_{d,n})=O(n^3)$, this gives $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-3}{3}, $$ by letting $n$ tend to infinity.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Height O(n^3) gives the even-d bound.

nodes.name: Odd case
nodes.statement: Let now $d$ be odd. Then we define $$ Q_{d,n}(x)=x(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-3,n}(x). $$ This polynomial has two close roots: $y_n$ and a root lying between $y_n$ and $w_{d-3,n}$. Thus we get $$ {\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-5}}, $$ for $n$ large enough, and $$ e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-5}{3}. $$ The proof of Theorem \ref{tm2} is complete.

nodes.statement_short: Odd d: multiply by x and use q_{d-3,n}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: In this section, we use the polynomials $p_{d,n}(x)$ to construct irreducible monic polynomials having two very close roots. Let $F_k$ denote the $k$th Fibonacci number defined by the recursion $F_0=0$, $F_1=1$ and $F_k=F_{k-1}+F_{k-2}$ for $k \ge 2$. Note that Fibonacci numbers appear in the asymptotic expansion of $x_n = (n+2) / (n^2 + 3n + 1)$, namely $$ x_n = 1/n-1/n^2+2/n^3-5/n^4+13/n^5-34/n^6+ \cdots - (-1)^k F_{2k-3}/n^{k} + \cdots $$ For $d\geq 0$, we first define monic polynomials $s_{d,n}(x)$ with a root close to $x_n $ by $$ s_{d,n} (x)=(-1)^{d-1}(F_{d-1}p_{d,n}(x) - F_d x p_{d-1,n} (x)), $$ and then monic polynomials with two close roots by $$ \eqalign{ r_{2d+1,n} (x) & = xs_{d,n}^2(x) + F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2 (x), \cr r_{2d,n}(x) & = s_{d,n}^2 (x) + F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2 (x). \cr} \eqno (5) $$ We claim that these polynomials are monic. It suffices to show that this is true for $s_{d,n}(x)$. Since the leading coefficient of $p_{d,n} (x)$ is $F_d n + F_{d-2}$, we deduce that the leading coefficient of $s_{d,n}(x)$ is equal to \begin{eqnarray*} & (-1)^{d-1} (F_{d-1}(F_d n + F_{d-2})-F_d(F_{d-1}n + F_{d-3})) \\ & = (-1)^{d-1}(F_{d-1}F_{d-2}-F_dF_{d-3}) = 1. \end{eqnarray*} From (2) we get $$ r_{2d+1,n}(x_n )=F_d^2/n^{4d-1} + O(1/n^{4d}) $$ and $$ r_{2d,n}(x_n )=F_{d-1}^2/n^{4d-3} + O(1/n^{4d-2}), $$ that is, $$ r_{d,n}(x_n )=F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2/n^{2d-3} + O(1/n^{2d-2}). $$ Observe that the degree of the polynomial $r_{d,n} (x)$ is $d$. We claim that $r_{d,n} (x)$ has two complex conjugate roots $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$ close to $x_n $, more precisely they are equal to $$ \eqalign{ 1/n-1/n^2+2/n^3- & 5/n^4+13/n^5- \ldots + \cr & + (-1)^d F_{2d-5}/n^{d-1} \pm i/n^{(2d-1)/2} + O(1/n^{d}). \cr} \eqno (6) $$ Indeed, the polynomials $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x)$ and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x)$ have double roots $y_{d+1,n}$ and $y_{d,n}$, resp., in the disc $|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d+1}$, resp. $|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d-1}$. Moreover, we have $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x) < xs_{d,n}^2(x)$ when $|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d+1}$ and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x) < s_{d,n}^2(x)$ when $|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d-1}$. Hence, by Rouch\'e's theorem, the polynomial $r_{d,n} (x)$ has two roots $v$ satisfying $|v-x_n |<1/n^{d-1}$. Using a complex version of Taylor's theorem, by writing the roots $v$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ close to $x_n$ as $v =x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ with $\gamma > 0$, we get $$ \eqalign{ 0 & =r_{d,n}(x_n +\beta+\gamma i) \cr & = r_{d,n}(x_n ) + (\beta+\gamma i)r'_{d,n}(x_n )+ (\beta+\gamma i)^2r''_{d,n}(x_n )/2+ O(1/n^{3d-5}). \cr} $$ Note that we have $$ r'_{2d+1,n}(x_n ) =\frac{2F_dF_{d+1}}{n^{2d-1}} + O(1/n^{2d}), $$ $$ r'_{2d,n}(x_n ) =\frac{2F_{d-1}F_{d-2}}{n^{2d-2}} + O(1/n^{2d-1}), $$ and $$ r''_{d,n}(x_n ) = 2F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 + O(n). $$ By considering imaginary parts in the above Taylor's formula we get \begin{eqnarray*} \beta &=& - \frac{r'_{d,n}(x_n)}{r''_{d,n}(x_n)} + O(\gamma^{-1}r''_{d,n}(x_n)^{-1}n^{-3d+5}) \\ &=& - \frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor + (-1)^d}}{n^d} + O\left(\frac{1}{n^{d+1}}\right) + O\left(\frac{1}{\gamma n^{3d-3}}\right). \end{eqnarray*} Since the distance between the roots $x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ and $x_n +\beta-\gamma i$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ is equal to $2 \gamma$ and $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, it follows from Mahler's theorem \cite{Mah64} quoted in the introduction that $\gamma \gg 1/n^{2d-2}$. Thus, $\beta = O(1/n^{d-1})$. Moreover, $\beta = O(1/n^d)$, unless $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$. Looking at real parts leads to $$ \eqalign{ \frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2}{n^{2d-3}} + \frac{2\beta F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor + (-1)^d}}{n^{d-2}} + (\beta^2 - \gamma^2) & F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 \cr & = O\left(\frac{1}{n^{2d-2}}\right).} \eqno{(7)} $$ The assumption that $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$ leads to a contradiction, by considering (7) as a quadratic equation in $\beta$. Hence, we have $\beta = O(1/n^{d})$. Now (7) gives $\gamma^2 = 1/n^{2d-1} + O(1/n^{2d})$, i.e., $\gamma = 1/n^{(2d-1)/2} + O(1/n^d)$, as claimed in (6). Let $R_{d,n}(x)$ be the irreducible factor of $r_{d,n}(x)$ having roots $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$. Denote by $\delta$ its degree. Note that, since $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, Gelfond's inequality implies that $$ H(R_{d,n})=O(n^2). \eqno (8) $$ Denote by ${\rm Res}_{d,n}$ the resultant of the polynomials $R_{d,n} (x)$ and $L_n(x)$. Since ${\rm Res}_{d,n}$ is a rational integer and $x_n$ is not a root of $R_{d,n} (x)$, we have $$ |{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \ge 1. \eqno (9) $$ Furthermore, the definition of the resultant of two polynomials (see e.g. \cite[p. 223]{BuLiv}) implies that (recall that $R_{d,n}(x)$ is monic) $$ |{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \le (n^2 + 3n+1)^{\delta} \prod_{t : R_{d,n} (t) = 0} \, |t - x_n|. $$ Since the product of the absolute values of all the roots of $R_{d,n} (x)$ different from $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$ is bounded from above by $\sqrt{d+1}$ times the height of $R_{d,n} (x)$ (see \cite[Exercise A.1]{BuLiv}), we deduce from (6) and (8) that $$ |{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \ll n^{2 \delta} n^{-2d+1} n^2. $$ Combined with (9), this gives $2 \delta \ge 2d - 3$, thus $$ \delta \in \{d, d-1\}. $$ This implies that either $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible, or it has an integer root (recall that any rational root of a monic polynomial must be a rational integer). Assume that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is reducible, i.e., that it has an integer root. This integer must divide $r_{d,n}(0)=F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2$, and, by (5), it is of the form $-\alpha^2$ for an integer $\alpha$ dividing $F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}$. So, for any given degree $d$, there are only finitely many possibilities for the integer root of $r_{d,n}(x)$. Write $r_{d,n}(x)$ as $$ r_{d,n}(x)=A_d(x)n^2+B_d(x)n+C_d(x). $$ By the definition of $r_{d,n}(x)$ and (1), it follows easily by induction that the discriminant $B_d(x)^2 - 4A_d(x)C_d(x)$ of $r_{d,n}(x)$ with respect to $n$ is equal to $-4 F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^4 x^{2d-1}$. In particular, this discriminant is nonzero at $x=-\alpha^2$, and thus at least one of the numbers $A_d(-\alpha^2)$, $B_d(-\alpha^2)$, $C_d(-\alpha^2)$ is nonzero. This shows that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[n,x]$. Furthermore, for given $\alpha$ there are exactly two (rational) values of $n$ such that $-\alpha^2$ is a root of $r_{d,n}(x)$. Hence, for sufficiently large positive integer $n$, the polynomial $r_{d,n}(x)$ has no integer roots, and therefore it is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Since $$ {\rm sep}(r_{d,n}) = O(n^{-(d-1/2)}), $$ we obtain $$ e_{{\rm irr}}^* (d) \geq \frac{2d-1}{4}, $$ which proves Theorem \ref{tm3}.

nodes.statement: Indeed, the polynomials $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x)$ and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x)$ have double roots $y_{d+1,n}$ and $y_{d,n}$, resp., in the disc $|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d+1}$, resp. $|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d-1}$. Moreover, we have $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x) < xs_{d,n}^2(x)$ when $|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d+1}$ and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x) < s_{d,n}^2(x)$ when $|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d-1}$. Hence, by Rouch\'e's theorem, the polynomial $r_{d,n} (x)$ has two roots $v$ satisfying $|v-x_n |<1/n^{d-1}$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Rouche's theorem gives two roots near x_n.

nodes.name: Taylor expansion
nodes.statement: Using a complex version of Taylor's theorem, by writing the roots $v$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ close to $x_n$ as $v =x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ with $\gamma > 0$, we get $$ \eqalign{ 0 & =r_{d,n}(x_n +\beta+\gamma i) \cr & = r_{d,n}(x_n ) + (\beta+\gamma i)r'_{d,n}(x_n )+ (\beta+\gamma i)^2r''_{d,n}(x_n )/2+ O(1/n^{3d-5}). \cr} $$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Taylor expansion at x_n with v=x_n+beta+gamma i.

nodes.name: Derivative asymptotics
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotics of r' and r'' at x_n.

nodes.name: Imaginary parts
nodes.statement: By considering imaginary parts in the above Taylor's formula we get \begin{eqnarray*} \beta &=& - \frac{r'_{d,n}(x_n)}{r''_{d,n}(x_n)} + O(\gamma^{-1}r''_{d,n}(x_n)^{-1}n^{-3d+5}) \\ &=& - \frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor + (-1)^d}}{n^d} + O\left(\frac{1}{n^{d+1}}\right) + O\left(\frac{1}{\gamma n^{3d-3}}\right). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Imaginary parts give beta.

nodes.name: Apply Mahler's bound
nodes.statement: Since the distance between the roots $x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ and $x_n +\beta-\gamma i$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ is equal to $2 \gamma$ and $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, it follows from Mahler's theorem \cite{Mah64} quoted in the introduction that $\gamma \gg 1/n^{2d-2}$. Thus, $\beta = O(1/n^{d-1})$. Moreover, $\beta = O(1/n^d)$, unless $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Mahler's bound gives gamma >> n^{-(2d-2)}, so beta small.

nodes.name: Real parts (7)
nodes.statement: Looking at real parts leads to $$ \eqalign{ \frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2}{n^{2d-3}} + \frac{2\beta F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor + (-1)^d}}{n^{d-2}} + (\beta^2 - \gamma^2) & F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 \cr & = O\left(\frac{1}{n^{2d-2}}\right).} \eqno{(7)} $$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Real parts give (7).

nodes.name: Solve for gamma
nodes.statement: The assumption that $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$ leads to a contradiction, by considering (7) as a quadratic equation in $\beta$. Hence, we have $\beta = O(1/n^{d})$. Now (7) gives $\gamma^2 = 1/n^{2d-1} + O(1/n^{2d})$, i.e., $\gamma = 1/n^{(2d-1)/2} + O(1/n^d)$, as claimed in (6).
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Solve (7) to get gamma, proving (6).

nodes.name: Irreducible factor
nodes.statement: Let $R_{d,n}(x)$ be the irreducible factor of $r_{d,n}(x)$ having roots $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$. Denote by $\delta$ its degree.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the irreducible factor R_{d,n} and its degree.

nodes.name: Gelfond's inequality
nodes.statement: Note that, since $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, Gelfond's inequality implies that $$ H(R_{d,n})=O(n^2). \eqno (8) $$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Gelfond's inequality bounds H(R_{d,n}).

nodes.name: Resultant lower bound
nodes.statement: Denote by ${\rm Res}_{d,n}$ the resultant of the polynomials $R_{d,n} (x)$ and $L_n(x)$. Since ${\rm Res}_{d,n}$ is a rational integer and $x_n$ is not a root of $R_{d,n} (x)$, we have $$ |{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \ge 1. \eqno (9) $$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: The resultant with L_n is a nonzero integer.

nodes.name: Resultant upper bound
nodes.statement: Furthermore, the definition of the resultant of two polynomials (see e.g. \cite[p. 223]{BuLiv}) implies that (recall that $R_{d,n}(x)$ is monic) $$ |{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \le (n^2 + 3n+1)^{\delta} \prod_{t : R_{d,n} (t) = 0} \, |t - x_n|. $$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound of the resultant by root distances.

nodes.name: Resultant estimate
nodes.statement: Since the product of the absolute values of all the roots of $R_{d,n} (x)$ different from $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$ is bounded from above by $\sqrt{d+1}$ times the height of $R_{d,n} (x)$ (see \cite[Exercise A.1]{BuLiv}), we deduce from (6) and (8) that $$ |{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \ll n^{2 \delta} n^{-2d+1} n^2. $$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Using (6) and (8) bound the resultant.

nodes.name: Degree of R_{d,n}
nodes.statement: Combined with (9), this gives $2 \delta \ge 2d - 3$, thus $$ \delta \in \{d, d-1\}. $$ This implies that either $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible, or it has an integer root (recall that any rational root of a monic polynomial must be a rational integer).
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Degree of R_{d,n} is d or d-1, so only an integer root can obstruct irreducibility.

nodes.name: Possible integer roots
nodes.statement: Assume that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is reducible, i.e., that it has an integer root. This integer must divide $r_{d,n}(0)=F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2$, and, by (5), it is of the form $-\alpha^2$ for an integer $\alpha$ dividing $F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}$. So, for any given degree $d$, there are only finitely many possibilities for the integer root of $r_{d,n}(x)$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: A possible integer root is -alpha^2 with alpha | F, finitely many options.

nodes.name: Irreducible over Z[n,x]
nodes.statement: Write $r_{d,n}(x)$ as $$ r_{d,n}(x)=A_d(x)n^2+B_d(x)n+C_d(x). $$ By the definition of $r_{d,n}(x)$ and (1), it follows easily by induction that the discriminant $B_d(x)^2 - 4A_d(x)C_d(x)$ of $r_{d,n}(x)$ with respect to $n$ is equal to $-4 F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^4 x^{2d-1}$. In particular, this discriminant is nonzero at $x=-\alpha^2$, and thus at least one of the numbers $A_d(-\alpha^2)$, $B_d(-\alpha^2)$, $C_d(-\alpha^2)$ is nonzero. This shows that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[n,x]$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Discriminant in n is nonzero, so r_{d,n} is irreducible over Z[n,x].

nodes.name: Irreducible over Z[x]
nodes.statement: Furthermore, for given $\alpha$ there are exactly two (rational) values of $n$ such that $-\alpha^2$ is a root of $r_{d,n}(x)$. Hence, for sufficiently large positive integer $n$, the polynomial $r_{d,n}(x)$ has no integer roots, and therefore it is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: For large n no integer root, so r_{d,n} irreducible over Z[x].

nodes.name: Conclude Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Since $$ {\rm sep}(r_{d,n}) = O(n^{-(d-1/2)}), $$ we obtain $$ e_{{\rm irr}}^* (d) \geq \frac{2d-1}{4}, $$ which proves Theorem \ref{tm3}.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: sep(r_{d,n})=O(n^{-(d-1/2)}) with height O(n^2) gives the bound.

nodes.name: Mahler's lower bound for clusters of roots
nodes.statement: Let $d \ge 2$ be an integer. Mahler's upper bound $e(d) \le d-1$ quoted in the Introduction is a particular case of the lower bound $$ \prod_{1\le i<j\le k} \vert \alpha_i -\alpha_j \vert \gg H(P)^{- d +1}, \eqno (10) $$ valid for any integer polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $d$ having at least $k \ge 2$ distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_k$, established in \cite{Mah64}.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
assumptions: valid for any integer polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $d$ having at least $k \ge 2$ distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_k$
nodes.statement_short: Mahler: the product of distances among any k distinct roots of an integer polynomial of degree d is >> H(P)^{-d+1}.

nodes.name: Mahler's cluster inequality
nodes.statement: \prod_{1\le i<j\le k} \vert \alpha_i -\alpha_j \vert \gg H(P)^{- d +1}, \eqno (10)
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots

nodes.name: Cluster exponents E(d,k) and E_irr(d,k)
nodes.statement: Let $k$ and $d$ be integers with $2 \le k \le d$. We denote by $E(d,k)$, respectively $E_{{\rm irr}}(d,k)$, the infimum of the real numbers $\delta$ for which $$ \prod_{1\le i<j\le k} \vert \alpha_i -\alpha_j \vert \ge H(P)^{- \delta} $$ holds for every integer polynomial $P(x)$, respectively, irreducible integer polynomial $P(x)$, of degree $d$ and sufficiently large height, with distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_d$.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
nodes.statement_short: E(d,k) (resp. E_irr) is the infimum of delta with prod of pairwise distances of k roots >= H(P)^{-delta} for all (irreducible) degree-d integer P of large height.

nodes.name: Monic cluster exponents E*(d,k) and E*_irr(d,k)
nodes.statement: We further use the notation $E^*(d,k)$, respectively $E_{{\rm irr}}^*(d,k)$, when we restrict our attention to monic integer polynomials, respectively monic integer irreducible polynomials.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots

nodes.name: Upper bound d-1 for cluster exponents
nodes.statement: We deduce from (10) that the quantities $E(d,k)$ and $E^* (d, k)$ are all bounded from above by $d-1$.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
conclusions: the quantities $E(d,k)$ and $E^* (d, k)$ are all bounded from above by $d-1$

nodes.name: Bugeaud-Mignotte cluster lower bounds
nodes.statement: Regarding lower bounds, it is proved in \cite{BM1,BM2} that, for any integer $d \ge 4$ and any integer $k\ge 2$ that divides $d$, we have $$ E(d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d \quad \mbox{and} \quad E^* (d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d - \frac{k-1}{2}. \eqno (11) $$
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
conclusions: E(d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d \quad \mbox{and} \quad E^* (d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d - \frac{k-1}{2}.

nodes.name: Known cluster lower bounds (11)
nodes.statement: E(d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d \quad \mbox{and} \quad E^* (d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d - \frac{k-1}{2}. \eqno (11)
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots

nodes.name: Bugeaud-Mignotte bounds hold for irreducible polynomials
nodes.statement: In fact, the results from \cite{BM1,BM2} show that these bounds are valid also for $E_{{\rm irr}} (d, k)$ and $E_{{\rm irr}}^* (d, k)$, respectively.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
conclusions: these bounds are valid also for $E_{{\rm irr}} (d, k)$ and $E_{{\rm irr}}^* (d, k)$, respectively

nodes.name: Theorem 4: lower bounds for clusters of roots
nodes.statement: For every integer $k \ge 3$, there exist rational numbers $c_1(k)$ and $c_2(k)$ such that, for every integer $d \ge k$, we have $$ E(d,k) \geq \frac{k}{k+1} d - c_1 (k) \eqno (12) $$ and $$ E^* (d,k) \geq \frac{k}{k+1} d - c_2 (k). \eqno (13) $$ In particular, the exponent $-d+1$ in (10) cannot be replaced by $- \alpha_k d$, for a real number $\alpha_k$ less than $k/(k+1)$, even if the polynomial $P(x)$ in (10) is assumed to be monic.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
conclusions: there exist rational numbers $c_1(k)$ and $c_2(k)$ such that, for every integer $d \ge k$, we have $$ E(d,k) \geq \frac{k}{k+1} d - c_1 (k) \eqno (12) $$ and $$ E^* (d,k) \geq \frac{k}{k+1} d - c_2 (k). \eqno (13) $$
the exponent $-d+1$ in (10) cannot be replaced by $- \alpha_k d$, for a real number $\alpha_k$ less than $k/(k+1)$, even if the polynomial $P(x)$ in (10) is assumed to be monic
nodes.statement_short: E(d,k) and E*(d,k) are at least kd/(k+1) minus a constant, so Mahler's exponent in (10) is nearly optimal even for monic P.

nodes.name: Cluster bound (12)
nodes.statement: E(d,k) \geq \frac{k}{k+1} d - c_1 (k) \eqno (12)
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots

nodes.name: Monic cluster bound (13)
nodes.statement: E^* (d,k) \geq \frac{k}{k+1} d - c_2 (k). \eqno (13)
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Let $\delta \ge 2$ and $h \ge 0$ be integers. The polynomial $$ {\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x) := P_{\delta, n} (x) \times p_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times p_{\delta+h, n} (x) $$ has degree $(h+2)\delta + h(h+1)/2$, height $\ll n^{h+4}$, and it has a cluster of $h+3$ roots close to each other. Setting $k = h+3$, a short calculation gives (12), since one can multiply ${\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x)$ by a suitable power of the monomial $x$. To get (13), it suffices, for $\delta$ even, to consider the polynomial $$ {\tilde Q}_{\delta, h, n} (x) := Q_{\delta, n} (x) \times q_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times q_{\delta + 2 h, n} (x), $$ multiplied by a suitable power of the monomial $x$. We omit the details.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
nodes.statement_short: Multiply P_{delta,n} by p_{delta,n},...,p_{delta+h,n} to get a cluster of h+3 close roots (and similarly with Q and q for monic); details omitted.

nodes.name: Cluster polynomial
nodes.statement: Let $\delta \ge 2$ and $h \ge 0$ be integers. The polynomial $$ {\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x) := P_{\delta, n} (x) \times p_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times p_{\delta+h, n} (x) $$ has degree $(h+2)\delta + h(h+1)/2$, height $\ll n^{h+4}$, and it has a cluster of $h+3$ roots close to each other.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
nodes.statement_short: Product polynomial with a cluster of h+3 close roots.

nodes.name: Derive (12)
nodes.statement: Setting $k = h+3$, a short calculation gives (12), since one can multiply ${\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x)$ by a suitable power of the monomial $x$.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
nodes.statement_short: A short calculation gives (12).

nodes.name: Derive (13)
nodes.statement: To get (13), it suffices, for $\delta$ even, to consider the polynomial $$ {\tilde Q}_{\delta, h, n} (x) := Q_{\delta, n} (x) \times q_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times q_{\delta + 2 h, n} (x), $$ multiplied by a suitable power of the monomial $x$. We omit the details.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
nodes.statement_short: Monic analogue with Q and q gives (13).
